sentences.text: Anchiceratops was a medium-sized, four-legged plant eater that grew to a length of 4.3 meters.
Its head featured three horns, including a parrot-like beak, with the brow horns being longer than the nose horn.
A long, rectangular frill with coarse triangular spikes lined the back of its skull.
The largest bone at the back of the frill nearly matched the height of the three bony plates running along the edge.
Pairs of bony bumps on the frill's edge varied wildly in shape and size between different individuals.
Barnum Brown first described the genus in 1914 after finding remains along the Red Deer River in Alberta in 1912.
Brown named the animal and viewed it as a transitional form between Monoclonius and Triceratops.
Flowering plants were uncommon, so the diet likely consisted mostly of conifers, cycads, and ferns.
In 2012, Mallon noted that Anchiceratops ornatus lived longer than other ceratopsids, possibly due to less competition or a generalist lifestyle.
Hadrosaurs were the most common dinosaurs in the region, making up half of all species present.
Brown placed the genus in Ceratopsia in 1914, and William Diller Matthew later assigned it to the family Ceratopsidae in 1915.
The animal belongs to the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
A second species, A. longirostris, named by Charles Mortram Sternberg in 1929, is now considered a synonym of A. ornatus.
This dinosaur lived between 73 and 68 million years ago in what is now Alberta, Canada.
Specimens are found in the Horsethief member of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation, dated to about 72 to 71 million years ago.
Researchers have concluded that differences in skull proportions among fossils represent different growth stages.
It is debated whether horn and frill fragments from the Oldman and Dinosaur Park Formations represent early A. ornatus or a second related species.
In 1959, Wann Langston Jr. suggested that Anchiceratops had a semi-aquatic lifestyle, using its long snout to cross swamps and its heavy frill as a counterbalance.
It has been proposed that Anchiceratops is a sexually dimorphic species, where the A. longirostris skull actually represents a female.
Skulls differ in proportions, such as supraorbital horn core size or frill dimensions, leading researchers to conclude the disparity results from interspecific differences or sexual dimorphism.
